web_evidence.title: Leon Uris Criticism: Uris, Leon
web_evidence.note: A reprinted Washington Post review identifies a recurring first-person narrator who disappears for long stretches and later reappears, describing the book's point-of-view discontinuity across its full span.

web_evidence.title: Leon Uris: A Critical Companion
web_evidence.note: Kathleen S. Cain's scholarly study states that Part One begins with eleven-year-old Seamus O'Neill's first-person narrative. This establishes the opening component only, not the whole-book configuration.

web_evidence.title: Leon Uris - Trinity
web_evidence.note: Searchable full text shows sustained Seamus first-person chapters and passages alternating with extended third-person scenes following Conor, the Hubbles, the Weeds, and other characters.

web_evidence.title: Trinity by Leon Uris
web_evidence.note: An explicit reader description independently reports that Conor is presented through a third-person narrator as well as occasional first-person accounts by Seamus O'Neill.

person_note: The novel alternates between sustained first-person narration by Seamus O'Neill and sustained third-person narration following Conor and other characters when Seamus is absent. q02171 directly exposes Seamus's participating we, while q02161 and q02170 belong to extended third-person sequences confirmed from surrounding text. Several other apparent first-person examples are dialogue or Daddo Friel's embedded historical speech and therefore do not identify the base narrator. Confidence is medium because the quote sample is sparse and only one Tier A/B source supports the exact ALTERNATING label; the Tier B evidence for a first-person opening is component evidence and does not satisfy a second exact-label source.
